analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA power to ban unsafe cosmetic chemicals, require full ingredient labels, and force recalls.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a House floor vote and died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, after being referred to two committees with one sponsor and four Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite federal cosmetics law, which barely regulates makeup, shampoo, lotion, and salon products. It would require the FDA to set a safety standard for every cosmetic ingredient, immediately ban a list of chemicals linked to cancer, hormone disruption, and birth defects (including formaldehyde-releasing preservatives, certain parabens, phthalates, lead acetate, and triclosan), force full ingredient disclosure including fragrance components and contaminants, give the FDA mandatory recall authority, require companies to report serious injuries, and ban animal testing. It also requires safety data sheets, in multiple languages, for products used by salon workers. Companies with over $10 million in sales would pay fees; small businesses under $2 million are exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses cosmetics and personal care products, which is nearly everyone. The biggest winners are the people most exposed: salon and nail salon workers (whom the bill specifically names as a highly exposed, vulnerable population), pregnant women, and children. Consumers would learn every ingredient in every product, including what is in fragrances, and a public FDA database would list safety data that companies currently keep to themselves. People harmed by products would benefit from mandatory company reporting of serious reactions and from FDA power to order a product pulled from shelves — authority the FDA does not have over cosmetics today.

how_it_helps.text: The bill deems about a dozen groups of ingredients prohibited on the day of enactment — including formaldehyde and formaldehyde-releasing preservatives, several parabens, DBP and DEHP phthalates, toluene, lead acetate, triclosan, coal tar dyes, and the sunscreen chemicals oxybenzone and octinoxate — because they fail the bill's safety standard [S3].

It requires full ingredient labels in order of concentration, including the components of fragrances (which are currently kept secret), contaminants above one part per billion, and ingredient lists on internet retailer pages [S3].
It gives the FDA authority to order a company to stop distributing and to recall a cosmetic that may cause a serious adverse event — recall power the agency lacks under current cosmetics law [S3].

Brand owners must report serious adverse events (death, hospitalization, miscarriage, hair loss, disfigurement) within 15 business days, and the reports become publicly available with personal details redacted [S3].

It sets a 'reasonable certainty of no harm' safety standard that specifically protects vulnerable populations — pregnant women, infants, children, the elderly, and highly exposed workers such as salon employees — and directs OSHA to require multilingual material safety data sheets for professional salon products, in English, Spanish, and Vietnamese [S3].
It bans animal testing for cosmetics, while carving out an exception where safety cannot be established with validated non-animal methods, and funds development of alternative test methods [S3].

Small businesses are protected: companies with under $2 million in annual cosmetic sales are exempt from registration and fees, fees apply only to companies above $10 million, and the FDA must provide technical support to small businesses [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large cosmetics and personal care companies, which would pay registration fees (only companies above $10 million in sales), submit safety data for every ingredient, test for contaminants, and reformulate products to remove banned or restricted chemicals. Some of those costs would be passed on to consumers through prices, and some products containing banned ingredients would disappear from shelves or need replacements.

drawbacks.text: The bill immediately bans chemicals the FDA currently approves, including oxybenzone and octinoxate, which are widely used sunscreen active ingredients; banning them by statute, without the FDA re-review process the bill itself creates for other ingredients, could reduce sunscreen options before safe substitutes are in place [S3].

The safety standard is extremely strict — no more than a one-in-a-million risk for any vulnerable population, or a 1,000-fold margin of safety counting cumulative exposure from all sources. Applied literally, it could force reformulation of a large share of products on the market and raise prices, and the deadlines (safety data for all existing products within one year) are tight [S3].

Requiring contaminants to appear on labels at levels above one part per billion could put trace amounts with no demonstrated health effect on labels, which may confuse rather than inform consumers and impose difficult detection and testing costs, especially on suppliers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Cosmetics are one of the least-regulated consumer product categories — before this bill, the FDA could not even force a recall of a dangerous lotion. The bill's core gains for consumers and salon workers are real and large, and the small-business exemptions and fee structure are well designed to spare small makers. The main honest objections are the design of the immediate-ban list (which pulls FDA-approved sunscreen actives without re-review) and a risk standard so strict it could disrupt many product lines. A more moderate version could capture most of the safety gains with less disruption; Congress eventually enacted a much narrower cosmetics modernization law in 2022 that included registration and adverse-event reporting but not the banned-ingredient list or mandatory recall power (general knowledge, not in the provided sources).

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Education and Workforce committees the day it was introduced, neither committee ever acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the Safe Cosmetics and Personal Care Products Act of 2018 on September 26, 2018 [S1][S3].
Four House Democrats cosponsored the bill, and no Republican did [S4].
The bill was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and to the Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day of introduction [S1][S5].
The action history shows no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action of any kind after the referral — the last entry in the record is the referral itself [S5].
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, so the bill expired with no vote ever taken [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cosmetics and personal care companies, which avoided registration fees, mandatory safety testing and data disclosure, reformulation to remove banned chemicals, and mandatory recall authority. Consumers and salon workers did not get the ingredient disclosure, banned-chemical list, or recall protections the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large cosmetics companies dodging new safety rules

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Safe Cosmetics and Personal Care Products Act of 2018 on September 26, 2018

against.name: Greg Walden
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; the committee took no action after the September 2018 referral, keeping the bill off the House floor

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call record, but the sponsorship was entirely one-party.

industries.industry: Cosmetics and personal care products manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would impose registration fees on companies above $10 million in sales, require submission and public disclosure of safety data, and force reformulation to eliminate banned ingredients like formaldehyde releasers, certain parabens, phthalates, and lead acetate. Companies' interest in avoiding these costs ran against consumers' interest in knowing what is in their products and in having dangerous products pulled from shelves.

Suppliers would have to disclose fragrance and preservative components (currently treated as trade secrets), test ingredients for contaminants, and provide safety data to brand owners within 90 days or face prohibitions. The bill explicitly strips trade-secret protection from ingredients required on labels.

industries.industry: Animal testing laboratories and contract research firms
industries.note: The bill bans animal testing for cosmetics development and bars the FDA from considering new animal-test data, allowing it only when safety cannot be established with validated non-animal methods. This aligns with widespread public support for ending animal testing.

Companies with under $2 million in annual cosmetic sales are exempt from registration and fees, and the bill directs the FDA to provide technical support to small businesses, shielding small and indie brands from most compliance costs.
